The Aasgard Pass approach is loose scree/talus gaining roughly 2000ft in under a mile; the descent rappels use climber-built slung anchors rather than fixed/bolted stations, so bring cordage to build or back these up
keep.overview: The classic South Face of Prusik Peak — one of the most celebrated alpine rock routes in the Enchantments, put up in 1968 by Ron Burgner and Fred Stanley.
keep.beta: Start near the middle of the south face base. Climb a wide crack/chimney (5.6-5.8), exit right on knobs into a deep gully, continue up the gully to a chockstone, tunnel behind it through steep double cracks, then finish through a flaring squeeze chimney (crux, 5.9+) and a left-facing corner to the summit.
keep.turnaround: Turn around if storms build over the Enchantments in the afternoon.
keep.rappels: Rappel the north face with slung/natural belay stations.
keep.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
keep.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Enchantment Basin or on the face; carry a satellite communicator.
keep.descent: Walk east from the summit and rappel the north face (about five single-rope rappels), then walk back around to the base.
obj_haz: loose rock near the chockstone tunnel
runout sections on the upper flare/chimney pitches
party traffic/queuing on a very popular line

waypoints.name: Aasgard Pass (Colchuck Pass)
waypoints.note: Steep, loose talus/scree (snow or ice into early summer) gaining roughly 2,200 ft in under a mile; watch for rockfall kicked down from parties above.

waypoints.name: Lake Viviane

waypoints.name: Gnome Tarn

waypoints.name: Chockstone squeeze / upper chimney (P5)
waypoints.note: Squirm through a tight hole behind a chockstone (awkward with a pack on) then work right into a slick, sparsely-protected 5.9+ chimney.

waypoints.name: Prusik Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit and top of the six-pitch, ~650 ft Burgner-Stanley line; small exposed perch at the west end of The Temple ridge.

waypoints.name: North face rappel descent
waypoints.note: Five rappels off slung blocks/horns down the north face, roughly an hour back to the base of the south face route where packs are typically stashed.

sectionBreakdown.note: Hike past Colchuck Lake and up Aasgard Pass into the core Enchantments, passing Tranquil, Isolation, and Perfection Lakes. Camp at Gnome Tarn, close to the south face.
Chimneys and corner systems for 6 pitches (~650 ft); pitches 1-2 and 3-4 link easily with a 60m rope. Car-to-car parties log about 5.5 hrs of pure climbing, then rappel the north face…
Break camp and hike back out over Aasgard Pass and past Colchuck Lake to the trailhead.

keep.detailed_rack: Single to double rack through hand size with a set of nuts to protect the continuous cracks.
pro_tips: Secure an Enchantments overnight permit well ahead — they're competitive by lottery.
Start the climb early to beat afternoon thunderstorms.
Savor the rock — it's some of the best in the range.
Expect a signature chockstone squeeze into a 70-ft chimney partway up, plus at least one full pitch of sustained off-width.
watch_out: Off-width sections can eat gear and time
Very popular — expect crowded belay ledges on summer weekends
keep.pro_needs: Standard crack rack; the line follows protectable crack systems on superb granite.
keep.best_season: Mid summer through early fall for dry, warm granite.
keep.approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, ascend Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles, roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's crux, hazardous under lingering snow into early July (hidden creek/moat beneath the talus) and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the pass (7,841 ft), travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, then contour below Prusik to the base of the south face and the start of the route — about 7.5–8 miles and 4,600 ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the final stretch. Overnight camping in the Core requires an Enchantments permit; a longer Snow Lakes Trail alternative exists when Aasgard Pass or the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead is closed.
keep.descent_text: Walk east from the summit and begin the north-face rappel line on slung belay stations — natural anchors (blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat); there's little to no fixed gear at the top. Plan on about five single-rope rappels, most around 25–30m, though the line can also be run with two ropes for fewer, longer rappels. Figure roughly an hour from the summit back to the base if the rap line isn't backed up with other parties, which does happen since several south-face routes share this descent. Bring extra tat to back up aged webbing on the natural anchors.
keep.bail: Rappel the route or descend the West Ridge; the main commitment is the long approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Wide crack (a #4 cam protects the crux size) and low fifth-class terrain up to trees; often combined with pitch 2.
Crack climbing exiting right on knobs, belaying at the highest trees before the gully.
Sustained gully climbing, belaying just below an obvious chockstone.
Steep double cracks lead to a tunnel behind the giant chockstone; belay at the top or in the squeeze chimney.
The flaring squeeze chimney crux — demanding for many parties, knee protection is useful; belay above on a ledge.
The 'amazing left-facing corner' pitch, sustained stemming on knobs, straight to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Core Enchantments overnight permits are competitive; fit parties without one sometimes push the whole route car-to-car in ~20-24 hrs instead.

Alpine-draw count is extrapolated from standard convention for a 6-pitch moderate route since no source gives an exact draw count. 2026-07-31: rock_grade corrected from 5.10a to 5.9+ and grade_num from 10 to 9 — contradicted this row's own top-level grade ("III, 5.9+") and pitch_detail (nothing above 5.9+); confirmed via Climbing.com's route title. 2026-07-31: dist_km corrected from 31.4 to 15.7 — was stored as a round-trip figure (matching this row's own itinerary.totalNote of "~19.5 mi round-trip") rather than the one-way convention the app doubles for display; both sibling Prusik Peak routes already store one-way distance.

rappel_detail.pull: The first pull is the one that jams — a party on this line had to free a stuck rope with a progress-capture pulley after the first rappel, and another watched the party ahead repeatedly hang ropes up on this face.
rappel_detail.notes: The shortest of the sequence; the four below it are near-full-length on a doubled 60 m.
rappel_detail.anchor: Fixed webbing at the true summit; no bolts and very little fixed gear anywhere on this route or at the top. What is present has been rebuilt — the rangers stripped the accumulated slings off the lower-summit stations in 2018, and a party that season found a home-made spinning hanger backed to a rock pinch at the true summit.
hazards: The start squeezes into a narrow chute and is awkward to commit to
Older, abandoned stations lie further climber's left and are not recommended
rappel_detail.station: From where the last corner pitch tops out, walk east along the summit to find the start of the north-face line. This is the same descent used by every South Face route on the peak, so expect to queue behind other parties.

rappel_detail.anchor: Webbing around a chockstone wedged between the main wall and a protruding flake. Moved off the big ledge in 2018.
hazards: Awkward, exposed perch that is hard to share comfortably
Aged webbing on a natural chockstone — inspect it and back it up with your own material rather than adding another sling to the pile
rappel_detail.station: Invisible from above — rappel roughly 25 m and look climber's left. It sits about 30 ft (9 m) climber's left of the old ledge station and about 50 ft (15 m) below it, so beta that sends you to a ledge will send you past it.
In plain sight directly below station 2 — the only station on the descent you do not have to hunt for.

rappel_detail.pull: Reported as having many places for the rope to get stuck — clear the strands off the alcove lip and gully edges before the last pull.
rappel_detail.notes: You can stop rappelling here and downclimb 3rd class ground climber's right to the climbers' trail.
hazards: Sits directly under a large amount of loose rock and is hard to leave without dislodging some of it onto whoever is below
Numerous rope-snagging features in the gully underneath
rappel_detail.station: Hidden. Trend climber's left off station 3 rather than straight down; it is in a small alcove left of station 3, immediately above the gully where the terrain relents to 3rd and 4th class.

rappel_detail.notes: From the trail, traverse west around the base of the peak to return to the foot of the South Face. Figure about an hour summit-to-base if nobody is queued ahead of you.
hazards: The alternative downclimb is loose
rappel_detail.station: Optional pair of stations climber's right of the gully below station 4, dropping straight onto the climbers' path and rejoining the old rappel line.

keep.rappel_count_note: About five single-rope rappels, depending on party choices; some parties run the same line with two ropes for fewer, longer rappels. Shared north-side descent used by multiple South Face routes on Prusik Peak, so expect traffic/queuing.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's left of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain to climber's right, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Rappel descent on the north side is shared by several south-face routes and backs up when busy
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse northeast to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of deep chimneys on the face. The route starts to the left of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep white granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just below some shrubby pines. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

drop.name: Stanley-Burgner
drop.fa: 1968; first ascent by Fred Stanley and Ron Burgner, nearly free except two points of aid for the leader.
hazards: Aasgard Pass approach involves loose scree/talus with roughly 2,000 ft of gain in under a mile; descent rappels use climber-built slung anchors, not bolted anchors.
drop.overview: The Enchantments' most celebrated moderate alpine rock line, put up in 1968 by Ron Burgner and Fred Stanley climbing directly up Prusik's south face to the summit — nearly free except two points of aid for the leader on the first ascent.
drop.beta: A Grade III alpine rock testpiece climbing straight up the obvious weakness in the south face — wide cracks and chimneys low, a tunnel behind a chockstone at mid-height, and a sustained crux corner high on the route.
drop.turnaround: With six sustained pitches, a chockstone tunnel, and a multi-rappel descent, parties should set a firm turnaround time and be ready to bail rather than get caught by afternoon storms high on the face.
drop.rappels: Rappel the north face with slung/natural belay stations, single or double rope.
drop.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
drop.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Enchantments Core Zone; carry a satellite communicator.
drop.descent: ~4 rappels down the north face (~1 hr), then walk back to camp/trail.
obj_haz: loose rock near the chockstone tunnel
runout sections on the upper flare/chimney pitches
party traffic/queuing on a very popular line

drop.approach: Access via the standard Core Enchantments approach: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) to the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft gain). Figure roughly an hour from the top back to the base of the route if no other parties are queued on the same rap line, which can get congested since this descent is shared by several south-face routes. Carry extra tat to back up aged slings on the natural anchors.
drop.bail: The chimney/gully system low on the route offers reasonable rappel/downclimb retreat from most stances; higher up, retreat means rappelling the same gear anchors used on the descent.

schedule.detail: P1 chimney or crack (5.7-5.8+) to a tree belay

schedule.label: Continue P2-P5
schedule.detail: Corner systems and a chockstone chimney (5.8-5.9)

schedule.label: Top out
schedule.detail: P6 strenuous crack/corner to the summit; ~5.5 hrs of climbing typical

schedule.detail: Rappel the north face, then walk back around to the base

days.note: Break camp and hike back out over Aasgard Pass and past Colchuck Lake to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip (~19.5 mi, ~6,000 ft round-trip) around Prusik's classic 6-pitch 5.9+ south-face line.

access.fees: Day-use: free. Overnight lottery: $6 non-refundable application fee, then $5/person/night if selected. (Some approaches — e.g. Mount Stuart via Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass — fall entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area and need only the free self-issue permit even overnight.)
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Day climbs: free self-issue day-use permit at the trailhead — no lottery needed. Overnight camping inside the Enchantment Permit Area boundary: Enchantments overnight lottery permit (Recreation.gov).
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601 off Icicle Creek Road)
road.status: Reached via paved Icicle Creek Road (FR 7600) about 8.5 miles from Leavenworth, then Eightmile Road (FR 7601) roughly 4 miles to the trailhead; the FR 7601 stretch is steep, narrow, and gets washboarded as the season progresses, so high-clearance is recommended.
road.driveNote: About 2.5 hours from Seattle via US-2 over Stevens Pass to Leavenworth, then 15-20 minutes up Icicle Creek Road; a Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or annual) is required to park, and a self-issued day-use wilderness permit or reserved overnight Enchantment Permit (lottery, May 15-Oct 31) is required beyond the trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: FR 7601 is gated and closed to vehicles each winter to protect the roadbed, reopening in late spring once snow clears; Aasgard Pass itself commonly holds snow and a hidden creek/moat hazard into early July.

climate.fall: Clear, cooler September conditions; shorter days.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the approach passes into June.
climate.summer: Warm and mostly stable, but watch for afternoon thunderstorms.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — deep snow/avalanche terrain on approach.
climate.typical: Dry East Cascades alpine-granite summer climate with afternoon convective storm risk.

emergency.notes: Cell coverage unreliable in the Core Zone; Chelan Co. Sheriff SAR is primary rescue responder.
emergency.rangerStation: Wenatchee River (Leavenworth) Ranger District, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA, (509) 548-2550
emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, 817 Commercial St, Leavenworth, WA — 24-hr ER, (509) 548-5815
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (emergency); RiverCom 911 regional dispatch; Chelan Co. Sheriff's Office non-emergency (509) 667-6851.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through mid-September, after Aasgard Pass melts out and before fall storms glaze the north-side rappels

July.reason: Aasgard sheds most of its snow during the month; early July can still mean firm morning snow on the pass and damp cracks after late storms.

June.reason: Aasgard Pass usually still holds steep snow needing axe and crampons, and snow lingers at the base of the north-side rappels off the summit.

August.reason: Dry fist cracks and a snow-free Aasgard Pass; the south face bakes in afternoon sun, and wildfire smoke can settle over the Enchantments.

October.reason: Larch crowds early, then cold rock, short days and the first snow on Aasgard and the north-side rappels; overnight permits still apply through October 31.

September.reason: Cool, dry granite on the south face and stable weather; the late-month larch season brings heavy day traffic up Aasgard.

gaps: GPS track sourced from public CalTopo map: https://caltopo.com/m/TK8J

rappel_detail.pull: Set the knot clear of the constriction and pull from directly below the station, not off to one side - the chute is what traps the strand.
rappel_detail.notes: First of four single-rope rappels down the north-face descent line.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung natural anchor (block/chockstone with tat); an old bolted station is also reported as an occasional alternative at the very top
hazards: The chute above the anchor is a rope-catcher; at least one party jammed the rope on this first pull and needed a progress-capture pulley to free it
rappel_detail.station: From the summit, walk east and drop onto the north face. Getting onto the first station is awkward - you squeeze into a small chute to reach it - and this is the shortest rappel of the sequence. An old bolted station is occasionally reported as an alternative right at the top.

hazards: Locating the stations, not the rappelling, is the crux of this descent; parties describe the raps themselves as easy but the sequence confusing
rappel_detail.station: Below the first drop, every station is a slung natural anchor - blocks and chockstones carrying webbing and tat, with little or no fixed gear. They are not stacked in a single fall line, so stop at the rope ends and look around before assuming you have overshot one.

hazards: The tat is whatever previous parties left and varies widely in age - carry cord and replace anything sun-bleached rather than backing it up and moving on
rappel_detail.station: Continues down the north-face line on the same style of slung natural station.

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching 3rd-class ledges/scree; traverse/scramble west back to the base of the route.
hazards: Parties who keep rappelling past the ledge end up off the established line on ground with no stations
rappel_detail.station: The last rappel puts you onto a good ledge system. From there traverse west and scramble down to the base of the route - do not go looking for further anchors below the ledge.

drop.rappel_count_note: The station count here is a rope-configuration question and all the published figures are right about different setups. On two ropes a party got down in three (two double-length rappels and one single). On a single 60 m rope doubled - a 30 m rappel - parties report four or five, one noting a shorter first rappel followed by four that were 30 m rope-stretchers, and that they 'probably could have done 4 and scrambled the 5th'. The four stations listed here are the single-rope sequence; if you are on 30 m rappels rather than 25 m, expect to reach the ledge in four or five, and treat the shorter first drop as normal.

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core Enchantments to the middle of the south face
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail two and a half miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Boulder-hop the east shore to the boulder field at the south end, then climb Aasgard Pass — about 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of steep loose scree, the physical crux of the approach. Into early July, snow can bridge a hidden creek and moat on the left side of the gully; that hazard has caused serious injuries and at least one death.

From the pass at about 7,800 ft, drop gently into the upper Core basin and travel cross-country north over slabs and heather past Isolation and Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, the usual bivy. The base of the south face is roughly fifteen to twenty minutes from there.

Overnight camping in the Core Zone needs a permit, so many parties do the whole thing in one long day instead.

When Aasgard or this trailhead is closed, the Snow Lakes trail is the longer alternative, reaching the same face past Lake Viviane.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is clear of the snow that bridges the creek beneath it
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose steep scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July with a fatal history
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the last stretch, with no tread
A flaring squeeze chimney at mid-height that is awkward with a pack
A shared north-side rappel descent that gets congested when several parties are on the face
Snafflehounds at the base and at bivy sites will chew boots and gear left out
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This is the route in the middle, and that is the first and most useful fact. Walking along the foot of the south face, the start sits at about the middle of the base. The lines on the left flank of the face all top out on the West Ridge; this one is the classic that goes to the actual summit.

The feature test: you are looking for a chimney system on steep white granite. Pitch one takes either a 5.6/5.7 chimney or a wide crack immediately left of that chimney, and lands on low fifth-class ground with trees on it. Trees at the top of your first pitch is a good confirmation.

How to tell it from its two neighbours, which is the actual problem on this face because three routes start within a hundred feet of each other:
  - If you can see two prominent V-shapes on the face and you are at a chimney to the left of them, you are at Beckey-Davis — one route too far right.
  - If you are about fifty feet left of where you think the standard line is, you are at Der Sportsman, and its first pitch is 5.11+ rather than 5.7. A first pitch that feels desperate is the loudest possible signal you are on the wrong route.

Starting coordinate, published for pitch one: roughly 47.48681, -120.78457. In fog with a GPS that is decisive; on a clear day the shape of the face is better.

And the arrival confirmation higher up: pitch five squeezes between a chockstone into a flaring chimney, and pitch six is a left-facing corner to the summit. If your route runs out on the West Ridge instead of the summit, you are on one of the left-flank lines.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8
